title: Who to Invite to Your Table (and How to Ask)
excerpt: Stop looking for strangers to evangelize. Look at the names already in your phone, and learn to ask in a way that opens a door instead of triggering an alarm.
body:
The first instinct of most new disciple-makers is to invite the wrong people in the wrong way. They scan their church for the most spiritually advanced person they can find, or they fixate on a hard case they barely know, and then they craft an invitation so loaded it sounds like a sales pitch. The person hears the pitch, smells the agenda, and says no.

Jesus did not work that way. He looked at the people already near him — a fisherman cleaning his nets, a tax collector at his booth — and he said, simply, "Follow me." The genius was not in his recruiting funnel. It was in his attention to the ordinary people already in his path.

## Start with your actual life

Make a list. Not a strategy, a list. Write down the people you already eat with, work beside, live near, text on a normal week. Your relatives. The couple two doors down. The guy from your shift. The friend who keeps asking real questions when everyone else stays shallow.

These are your people. Acts describes the gospel moving along the lines of existing relationship — household to household, oikos to oikos. You are not being asked to manufacture closeness with strangers. You are being asked to bring Jesus into the closeness you already have.

Now look at that list and notice three kinds of people.

## The hungry

Some people are visibly hungry for more than they are getting. The Christian whose faith has outgrown the answers they were handed at twelve. The new believer who keeps saying "I want to grow but I don't know how." The person who lingers after church because they don't want the conversation to end. Invite the hungry first. They will carry the table when you are tired, and they will multiply it faster than you expect.

## The near

Some people are not hungry yet but are near. The neighbor you wave to. The coworker you trust. They are not asking spiritual questions, but they are not closed either. They will come for the meal and the company long before they come for the Bible, and that is fine. Jesus ate with people who were nowhere near a decision, and the eating was not a tactic. It was love.

## The skeptic

And some people doubt. Do not avoid them. I came to faith out of atheism, and the thing that moved me was not an argument shouted at a distance — it was being let into a room where honest belief was lived in front of me without flinching. A skeptic at your table is not a threat to it. Often he is the reason it stays honest.

## How to ask

Here is where most people fail. They over-explain. They turn a simple invitation into a paragraph that announces a commitment, a curriculum, and an altar call, and the person quietly backs away.

Keep it short and concrete. "A few of us are eating together on Tuesday nights and reading some of the Bible and praying. No pressure, no performance. Would you come this week?" Name the night. Name the meal. Name that it's low-key. Then stop talking.

Ask in person or by a real message, not a group blast. A group invitation feels like an event. A personal one feels like being wanted, and being wanted is what gets people in the door.

## Expect some noes

Not everyone will come. The rich young ruler walked away from Jesus himself (Mark 10:22), so you are in good company when someone declines. A no is not a verdict on you or on them. People say no because the timing is wrong, the week is full, or they're scared of what they think you're offering. Leave the door open. Ask again in a month. Some of my most faithful table members said no the first time and yes the third.

## Don't curate too tightly

Resist the urge to build a perfect group. The temptation is to invite only people like you — same age, same season, same politics — and call the comfort "unity." But the table that changes people is usually mixed. The older believer and the young doubter. The married couple and the single guy. The mess of it is the point. Paul told the Romans to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them (Romans 15:7), and Christ did not welcome only the convenient.

## This week

Make the list. Twelve names, more if they come. Circle three: one hungry, one near, one who doubts. Then ask all three, in person or by a personal message, using fewer words than you want to. Name the night. Name the meal. Then trust that the same Jesus who said "Follow me" to fishermen is still the one doing the calling.

You are not assembling an audience. You are answering a command with the names already in your phone.
